newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean unions end indefinite strike, arrest made.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean unions end indefinite strike, arrest made.

text.p: South Korean strike leaders on Saturday abandoned calls for indefinite stoppages in protest at a controversial labour law and said they would limit their industrial action.

Police arrested a shipyard unionist in the southeastern city of Ulsan, bringing to five the number of union heads picked up since South Korean courts last week issued warrants for the arrest of 20 labour leaders.
In a sign union bosses were wilting under pressure, the leader of the outlawed Korean Confederation of Trade Unions said its members would return to work on Monday.
"From next week, full strikes will take place only on Wednesday. On other week days, union members will work normally," Kwon Young-kil told a news conference.
"Every Saturday we will hold protest rallies after work."
But Kwon warned of an "all-out struggle" from February 18 unless the government promised to revise the labour law, which allows companies to lay off workers and replace strikers.
Kwon and six deputies, who have led more than three weeks of stoppages that have now largely tapered off, are sheltering from arrest at Myongdong Cathedral in central Seoul.

The government has heaped pressure on the fugitives, keeping a tight security noose around the church. Riot police guarded approaches to the cathedral on Saturday, checking cars in an apparent bid to stop union activists slipping in or out.
In Ulsan, police arrested Kim Il-shik, confederation leader of Hyundai Heavy Industries, the country's largest shipyard, in an early morning raid.
Police said Kim was charged with obstructing business.

Earlier this week four union officials from Halla Heavy Industries were arrested on similar charges. State prosecutors have warned the strike leaders they faced arrest unless they dropped industrial action immediately.
An aide to Kwon said the confederation was changing tactics to prolong the protests, aiming more at a political struggle.
"If it is impossible to force this government to revise the law then we will have to oust it in the next election and seek a revision by a new ruling camp," he said.
South Korea is due to hold presidential elections in December. President Kim Young-sam is limited to one term.
Nearly 10,000 people, many of them waving black cloth to symbolise the "death of democracy", held a noisy rally in a Seoul park to demand Kim's resignation.
Kim's popularity has plunged since his ruling New Korea Party rammed the labour bill through parliament in a dawn session on December 26 while opposition deputies slept.
He has refused to revise or revoke the law, arguing labour reform is crucial to trim corporate costs and improve international competitiveness.
Seizing on public dismay at the forced passage of the law, the opposition has thrown its weight behind union leaders.
Groups of opposition politicians, including main leader Kim Dae-jung and a number of parliamentarians, collected signatures in Seoul on Saturday to demand the government repeal the law.
Labour Ministry officials said on Saturday the strikes had faded. The ministry said some 30,000 workers were on strike.
The confederation provided no comparative turnout.
Highlighting that only pockets of resistance remain, Hyundai Motor Co Ltd, the nation's largest carmaker, reopened on Saturday after a week of temporary shutdowns.
Kwon denied a report by the state-run Korea Broadcasting System which said the confederation would halt strikes completely if implementation of the law was delayed.
On Friday, the ruling New Korea Party scorned Kwon's acceptance of an offer for a televised debate over the law, saying it could not deal with a wanted man.
